items.title: Know Your State
items.author: Omoseindemi Olobayo
items.excerpt: Building the intelligence infrastructure that lets a state plan with precision, include everyone, and earn its own way.

image.alt: A canoe on the Lagos lagoon at dusk, with a lit bridge and the city skyline

body: Most states plan, tax and invest with a partial, dated view of their own economy.
The answer is permanent intelligence infrastructure: verified data on six kinds of place, read by AI that answers leaders in plain words.

items.text: Most states plan, tax and invest with a partial, dated view of their own economy.

sections.title: The Potential
sections.lead: A state that cannot see its economy cannot grow it, tax it fairly, or sell it to investors.

paragraphs: State IGR reached about NGN 4.15 trillion in 2025. Lagos alone raised about 45% of it. The lowest-earning states raised between NGN 15 billion and NGN 21 billion each. The distance is not only economic size. It is also how well each state can see, measure and act on its own economy.

Lagos shows what visibility is worth. The state tied an 18.5% rise in IGR in 2025 to digital reforms, including geo-tagging and linking tax records to company registration data. Most states do not yet have that picture. Much of their economy, from markets to motor parks, is informal and uncounted.

blocks.caption: The IGR gap between Nigerian states, NGN billion, 2025. The other-state average is calculated from the 2025 aggregate of about NGN 4.147 trillion. Source: BudgIT data, analysed by BusinessDay.

items.title: Revenue unseen
items.text: Businesses and assets that exist, and appear in no record.

items.title: Investment lost
items.text: Investors choose states that can show them evidence.

items.title: Spending that misses
items.text: Programmes reach the visible, not the neediest.

blocks.title: The prize
blocks.text: The most comprehensively understood state in Nigeria, and the first to turn that knowledge into revenue.

sections.title: The Idea
sections.lead: Permanent intelligence infrastructure: a living picture of the state that leaders can question, and that earns its keep.

items.label: Capture
items.title: Field and existing systems
items.text: Verified, time-stamped field capture. MDA records for tax, residents and land. Maps and satellite for land use and flood risk. Telecom and payments, aggregated only. Citizen reports, verified and rewarded.

items.label: Reason
items.title: One state picture
items.text: Verified data, scored for accuracy. A knowledge graph of places, people and flows. AI synthesis that answers in plain words.

items.label: Use and earn
items.title: Decisions, then revenue
items.text: Briefs and alerts for the executive council. Planning, targeting and budgets for MDAs. A full base for the revenue service. Subscribers who pay for insight and APIs.

blocks.title: Ownership
blocks.text: The state owns the data. Personal data is never sold.

items.title: Markets and business clusters
items.text: Revenue, jobs, trade and digital adoption.

items.title: Informal settlements
items.text: Housing, sanitation, water, health and schooling.

items.title: Motor parks and corridors
items.text: People and goods, safety and levies.

items.title: Residential estates
items.text: Power, waste, security and whether services hold.

items.title: Social and civic places
items.text: Schools, clinics and community venues.

items.title: Economic and coastal zones
items.text: Ports, industry, tourism and climate risk.

paragraphs: Together, the six kinds of place show how people in the state live, move, trade and connect, mapped to every pillar of the state development plan.

Dashboards show what happened. Synthesis explains why, and what to do next. Leaders ask in English, Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo or Pidgin, by web, mobile, WhatsApp or USSD. Every answer shows its sources and how confident it is.

blocks.caption: Seven questions a state can finally answer.
rows: Descriptive
What is happening?
How many children are out of school, and where are they?
Diagnostic
Why is it happening?
Why do some markets earn far more than others?
Comparative
How do places differ?
How does service access in settlements compare with estates?
Predictive
What will happen?
If transport costs rise 20%, what happens to market prices?
Prescriptive
What should we do?
Where should new clinics go to reach the most underserved?
Impact
Did it work?
Did the drainage project cut flooding and illness?
Equity
Who is left behind?
Where is the earnings gap between women and men widest?

items.title: Gender
items.text: Every measure is broken down, so the average is not the only number.

items.title: Age
items.text: Children, working age and older people stay visible in the same picture.

items.title: Disability
items.text: Access is counted for people the average would hide.

items.title: Income
items.text: The test of success: the poorest fifth of communities improves faster than the richest fifth.

items.title: Location
items.text: A ward can be seen against the state, not only as a line in a state total.

blocks.title: What it is not
blocks.text: Not a surveillance system, not a sale of personal data, and not another dashboard nobody opens.

sections.title: Why It Matters Now
sections.lead: Four shifts make this the right year to build, and waiting costs more each year.

items.title: Revenue must come from within
items.text: With the national tax reforms signed in 2025 and pressure on federal allocations, a state needs its own revenue base. That base has to be measured before it can grow.

items.title: AI makes synthesis affordable
items.text: Work that once took an analyst team months, such as reading surveys, audits and records together, can now be done in minutes and asked in plain words.

items.title: Investors ask for evidence
items.text: Capital compares states on data. A state that can show demand, footfall and infrastructure gaps wins the meeting.

items.title: Cities outgrow their maps
items.text: Fast urban growth means the last census is already wrong. Informal settlements and markets change faster than records do.

paragraphs: In most states the planning cycle still runs plan, budget, spend, survey, report, shelve. Each survey is a one-off. The next plan starts from data already years old. The state pays again to learn what it once knew.

blocks.title: Funders are already backing this kind of infrastructure
blocks.text: In February 2026, officials in Andhra Pradesh briefed Bill Gates on the state's data lake and real-time governance centre.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.lead: The parts are proven elsewhere, and the field method is proven here.

blocks.caption: Four precedents, and what they teach.
rows: Andhra Pradesh, Real-Time Governance Society
By 2026 its state data lake joined 55 databases across 41 departments and agencies.
Run it from the centre of government.
Lagos State, digital tax reform
Tax revenue rose from NGN 678 billion in 2023 to NGN 1.44 trillion in 2025, which the state credited to digital reforms.
Better data moves revenue.
Great Britain, Ordnance Survey
A government-owned company whose map data serves more than 5,000 organisations.
Authoritative public data can be a business.
European Union, public sector information
Direct economic value of reused public data is projected to grow from EUR 52 billion in 2018 to EUR 194 billion by 2030.
Value grows every time data is reused.

blocks.caption: Lagos State tax revenue, NGN billion. Source: Lagos State Ministry of Finance, ministerial press briefing, May 2026. The same briefing reported state IGR of NGN 1.58 trillion in 2024 and NGN 1.87 trillion in 2025.

paragraphs: Softcom's Know Lagos pilot gathered data in markets, informal settlements and motor parks, the hardest places in a megacity to count. Every record is time-stamped, location-checked and scored for accuracy, then accepted or rejected in real time. Statewide rollout waits until accuracy passes 90%.

blocks.title: The leader's dividend
blocks.text: Leave behind a state that knows itself. Projects end with an administration. A state's knowledge of itself keeps paying back to whoever governs next.

blocks.title: Field note
blocks.text: The first question matters more than the first dashboard. Pick one decision the Governor must make this quarter and answer it with evidence no one had before. That single answer wins more support than any launch event.

sections.title: What Success Requires
sections.lead: Five conditions, a 36-month roadmap, and results you can hold us to.

items.title: A sponsor at the top
items.text: A steering committee led by the planning commissioner reports to the Governor every quarter.

items.title: A data-sharing order
items.text: An executive order and MOUs require every MDA to share data on common standards.

items.title: Anchors signed early
items.text: About 12 anchor companies commit before field work begins.

items.title: Independent oversight
items.text: A governance board with civil society, an ethics committee and a privacy officer, under the NDPA 2023.

items.title: A quality gate
items.text: No statewide rollout until field data passes 90% accuracy.

items.label: Months 1 to 6
items.title: Foundation
items.text: Governance in place. 50 enumerators trained. A pilot in 7 places. A working platform. Anchor partners signed.

items.label: Months 7 to 18

items.label: Months 19 to 36
items.title: Maturity
items.text: Full statewide coverage. Repeat surveys that track change. Early-warning alerts. A platform that sustains itself.

items.title: Quality
items.text: Data accuracy and freshness.

items.title: Cost covered

items.title: Why Digital Transformation Fails in African Enterprises — And What to Do About It
items.excerpt: Most digital transformation efforts fail not because of bad technology, but because of a fundamental misreading of what needs to change.

image.alt: A market trader smiling at her phone beside her stall

body: Across Nigeria and the broader African continent, the story repeats itself with uncomfortable regularity. A large enterprise — bank, telco, retailer, or government agency — announces a major digital transformation initiative. External consultants are brought in. A global platform is selected. Millions are committed. And then, two or three years later, the system sits half-implemented, the champions have moved on, and the organisation reverts to what it was doing before.

The failure is rarely technological. The platforms being deployed — whether ERP systems, core banking software, CRM tools, or data platforms — are mature, tested, and capable. The failure is almost always organisational. It is a failure to change the workflows, incentive structures, and mental models that the technology is supposed to serve. A digital system layered onto an analogue process does not produce a digital process. It produces an expensive, underused system and a frustrated workforce.

There are three patterns we see most consistently in failed transformations. The first is scope without sequence — organisations try to change everything at once and end up changing nothing. The second is technology without redesign — new tools are deployed without rethinking the underlying processes they are supposed to improve. The third is implementation without ownership — transformation programmes are run by external teams with no accountability for outcomes after go-live.

What works is different. Successful transformations in African enterprises share a common thread: they start small, move deliberately, and are owned internally at a senior level. They treat the first phase as a learning exercise, not a solution deployment. They build internal capability alongside external delivery. And they define success not by go-live, but by measurable improvement in operational outcomes — faster service, lower cost, better decisions.

For Softcom, this insight has shaped how we engage. We do not sell transformation as a destination. We design it as a journey — one with clear phases, internal champions, and outcomes we stay accountable for long after the initial deployment.
